<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:extreme point}
Let $y\in\{0,1\}^{T}$ and let $x$ be an extreme point of $\mathcal{X}(y)$. Then every regeneration interval associated with $x$ contains at most one partially utilized production period.

In other words, except for at most one period in each regeneration interval, every production quantity belongs to $\mathcal{B}_t:=\{0,L_t,U_t\}$.
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Fix an arbitrary setup vector
$y\in\{0,1\}^{T}$ and an extreme point
$x\in X(y)$.

Consider a regeneration interval $(\ell,r]$
associated with $x$. Suppose, by contradiction,
that two distinct periods $i$ and $j$, with
$\ell<i<j\le r$, are partially utilized. Thus, $L_i y_i < x_i < U_i y_i$ and  $L_j y_j < x_j < U_j y_j$.
 

For a scalar $\theta$, define the perturbed
production vector $x(\theta)$ by $x_i(\theta)=x_i+\theta$ and $x_j(\theta)=x_j-\theta$,  leaving all other production quantities unchanged.

This perturbation preserves total production
and leaves cumulative production unchanged from
period $j$ onward. For $t=i,\ldots,j-1$,
cumulative production becomes $P_t(\theta)=P_t+\theta$.
 

Since these periods lie strictly inside the
regeneration interval, we have $P_t>D_t$.
Moreover, both $x_i$ and $x_j$ lie strictly
between their respective production bounds.

Consequently, there exists $\varepsilon>0$
such that both $x(\varepsilon)$ and
$x(-\varepsilon)$ belong to $X(y)$.

These vectors are distinct, and $x=\frac12 x(\varepsilon)
  +\frac12 x(-\varepsilon)$, contradicting the assumption that $x$ is an
extreme point of $X(y)$.

Therefore, every regeneration interval contains
at most one partially utilized production period.

All remaining production quantities lie on their
respective bounds, so that $x_t\in\{0,L_t,U_t\}$. This completes the proof.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:main-grid}
There exists an optimal solution of problem~$\mathcal P$ whose cumulative production trajectory satisfies $P_t\in G_t$ for all $t\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{0\}$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:extreme point}, there exists an optimal solution such that every regeneration interval contains at most one partially utilized production period.

Consider such an optimal solution and an arbitrary regeneration interval $(\ell,r]$. By definition, $P_\ell=D_\ell$ and $P_r=D_r$.  Suppose first that the regeneration interval contains a partially utilized period $k$.

Consider a period $t$ satisfying $\ell\leq t<k$.  Since the unique possible partially utilized period is $k$, every production quantity in $\{\ell+1,\ldots,t\}$ belongs to its corresponding boundary set. Hence, $x_u\in\mathcal{B}_u$ for all $u=\ell+1,\ldots,t$. 
 
Using the left endpoint of the regeneration interval gives
\begin{equation*}
P_t
=
P_\ell+
\sum_{u=\ell+1}^{t}x_u
=
D_\ell+
\sum_{u=\ell+1}^{t}x_u. 
\end{equation*}
Therefore, $\sum_{u=\ell+1}^{t}x_u
\in
\mathcal{A}(\{\ell+1,\ldots,t\})$,  and consequently $P_t\in G_t^{+}$.
 

Now consider a period $t$ satisfying $k\leq t\leq r$. Using the right endpoint of the regeneration interval,
\begin{equation*}
P_t
=
P_r-
\sum_{u=t+1}^{r}x_u
=
D_r-
\sum_{u=t+1}^{r}x_u. 
\end{equation*}
Since $t\geq k$, the possibly partially utilized period $k$ does not appear in the sum on the right-hand side. Hence, $x_u\in\mathcal{B}_u$ for all $u=t+1,\ldots,r$,  so that $\sum_{u=t+1}^{r}x_u
\in
\mathcal{A}(\{t+1,\ldots,r\})$. It follows that $P_t\in G_t^{-}$. 
 
Suppose now that the regeneration interval contains no partially utilized production period. Then every production quantity in the interval belongs to its corresponding boundary set. For every $t\in\{\ell,\ldots,r\}$,
\begin{equation*}
P_t
=
D_\ell+
\sum_{u=\ell+1}^{t}x_u, 
\end{equation*}
and therefore $P_t\in G_t^{+}$. 
 
Thus, in all cases, $P_t\in G_t^{+}\cup G_t^{-}$. Moreover,  feasibility additionally implies $D_t\leq P_t\leq D_T$.  Hence,
\begin{equation*}
P_t\in
\left(
G_t^{+}\cup G_t^{-}
\right)
\cap[D_t,D_T]
=
G_t.
\end{equation*}

Since the argument applies to every regeneration interval, we obtain $P_t\in G_t$ for all $t\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{0\}$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
There exists an optimal solution of problem~$\mathcal P$ satisfying $P_t\in G$ for all $t\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{0\}$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- example-1: body_md -->
\label{ex:exponential-grid}

Consider the special case $L_t=0$ and $U_t=C_t$,  with $C_t=2^{T-t}$ for all $t\in\mathcal{T}$. Thus, $C_1=2^{T-1},\ 
C_2=2^{T-2}, 
\ldots, 
C_T=1$. 
 

Suppose that demand occurs only in the final period and equals total
available capacity, i.e., $d_t=0$ for all $t\in\mathcal{T}-1$, and $d_T
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}C_t
=
2^T-1$.   Then $D_0=D_1=\cdots=D_{T-1}=0$. 
 

Consider the positive grid at period $T-1$. Since $\mathcal{B}_t=\{0,C_t\}$,  we have
\begin{equation*}
G_{T-1}^{+}
\supseteq
\left\{
\sum_{u\in S}C_u
:
S\subseteq\{1,\ldots,T-1\}
\right\}. 
\end{equation*}

Because $C_1,\ldots,C_{T-1}$ are distinct powers of two, every subset produces a different sum.
Consequently, $|G_{T-1}|
\geq
2^{T-1}$.

Hence, the additive grid may have exponential cardinality.
<!-- end example-1 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:grid-dp}
The dynamic programming recurrence
\eqref{eq:grid-dp-recurrence} returns the optimal value of
problem~$\mathcal P$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
We first consider the problem restricted to cumulative production
trajectories satisfying $P_t\in G_t$ for all $t\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{0\}$. 
 

For $t=0$, the only feasible cumulative production level is $P_0=0$,
so the initialization is correct. 

Assume that the dynamic programming values are correct at the end of
period $t-1$, and consider a state $s\in G_t$. Every feasible partial
solution ending at $s$ has a predecessor $r=P_{t-1}\in G_{t-1}$,  and produces $x_t=s-r$.  The transition is feasible precisely when $x_t=0$ or $L_t\leq x_t\leq U_t$ for $x_t>0$. Its additional cost is $\phi_t(x_t)+h_t(s-D_t)$.  Taking the minimum over all feasible predecessors therefore gives
exactly recurrence~\eqref{eq:grid-dp-recurrence}.

Therefore, by induction, $F_T(D_T)$ is the optimal value among all feasible
solutions whose cumulative production levels belong to the grids. Moreover,  by the MGT,  restricting the dynamic program to the additive grids causes no loss of optimality. Thus, the solution of the dynamic program is optimal.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:grid-dp-complexity}
Assume that the period-dependent grids $G_0,\ldots,G_T$ are given and sorted. Then the GDP algorithm can be implemented in
\begin{equation}
O
\left(
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
(N_{t-1}+N_t)
\right)
\subseteq
O(TN)
\label{eq:accelerated-complexity}
\end{equation}
time and $O(N)$ working memory for computing the optimal value.
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Fix a period $t$. The states of $G_t$ and the predecessor states of $G_{t-1}$ are scanned in increasing order.

For the positive production term in \eqref{eq:accelerated-recurrence}, a monotone deque maintains the minimum of $F_{t-1}(r)-p_t r$ over the moving window $W_t(s)$. Each point of $G_{t-1}$ is inserted into the deque at most once and removed at most once. Hence, evaluating all positive production transitions in period $t$ requires $O(N_{t-1}+N_t)$ time. The zero-production term $\overline{F}_{t-1}(s)$ can be evaluated during the same ordered scan. Summing over all periods gives~\eqref{eq:accelerated-complexity}. 

Only two consecutive dynamic programming layers and the monotone deque need to be stored when only the optimal value is required. Each contains at most $O(N)$ values, yielding the stated working-memory bound. If a predecessor is stored for every finite state in order to recover an optimal solution without recomputation, the corresponding storage is $O(\sum_{t=0}^{T}N_t)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:grid-envelope}
A finite set $H\subseteq[0,D_T]$ is called a \emph{grid envelope} for an instance $I$ if $G\subseteq H$.
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:grid-enlargement}
Let $H$ be a grid envelope. If the GDP algorithm is applied using $H\cap[D_t,D_T]$ in period $t$, then it returns the optimal value of problem~$\mathcal P$.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Since $G\subseteq H$, the MGT guarantees the existence of an optimal solution whose cumulative production trajectory is entirely contained in $H$. Since $G_t\subseteq[D_t,D_T]$, this trajectory is also contained in $H\cap[D_t,D_T]$ in every period $t$.

Conversely, every finite-cost path considered by the dynamic program satisfies the original production boundary and inventory constraints. The restriction $s\geq D_t$ ensures nonnegative inventory, while the transition conditions enforce production feasibility.
Thus, enlarging the grid may introduce additional states, but it cannot introduce a solution with an objective value smaller than the true optimum.

Hence, the dynamic program over $H$ contains at least one optimal trajectory and returns the optimal value.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:polynomial grid-condition}
A family $\mathfrak{I}$ of dynamic lot-sizing instances is said to satisfy the \emph{polynomial grid condition} if there exists a polynomial $q$ such that, for every instance $I\in\mathfrak{I}$, one can construct in time polynomial in $\langle I\rangle$, a grid envelope $H(I)$ satisfying $|H(I)|\leq q(\langle I\rangle)$, with all grid values represented exactly.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:polynomial grid-principle}
Every family of instances satisfying the polynomial grid condition is
solvable in polynomial time by the GDP algorithm.
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Let $H(I)$ be the grid envelope provided by
Definition~\ref{def:polynomial grid-condition}, and set $N_H:=|H(I)|$.  By assumption, $N_H$ is polynomially bounded in $\langle I\rangle$,
and the grid can be generated in polynomial time.

A polynomial number of rational grid points can also be sorted in
polynomial time. By Proposition~\ref{prop:grid-dp-complexity}, the
dynamic programming phase requires $O(N_H\log N_H+TN_H)$ time when the common grid implementation is used. Since $T$ is polynomially bounded by $\langle I\rangle$ and $N_H$ is polynomially bounded, the complete algorithm runs in polynomial time.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:additive-representation}
A family of boundary resource profiles is said to admit a
$p$-dimensional additive representation if there exist fixed
nonnegative integers $c_1,\ldots,c_p$, independent of the planning horizon, such that every profile in the
family admits rational basis values $\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_p$ and integer-valued coordinate maps $g_i(t,b)$,  with $i=1,\ldots,p$, $t\in\mathcal{T}$, and $b\in\mathcal{B}_t$,   satisfying
\begin{equation}
b
=
\sum_{i=1}^{p}
\theta_i g_i(t,b),
\qquad
t\in\mathcal{T},
\quad
b\in\mathcal{B}_t,
\label{eq:additive-representation}
\end{equation}
with $|g_i(t,b)|
\leq
T^{c_i}$ for all $i=1,\ldots,p$, and we additionally set $g_i(t,0)=0$ for all $i=1,\ldots,p$. 
 
We further require that the basis values $\theta_i$ and the coordinates $g_i(t,b)$ can be computed in time polynomial in the binary encoding length of the instance, and that their binary encoding lengths are polynomially bounded.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:additive dimension}
The \emph{additive dimension} of a family of boundary resource
profiles, denoted by $\operatorname{adim}(\mathcal{B})$,  is the smallest integer $p$ for which the family admits a
$p$-dimensional additive representation in the sense of
Definition~\ref{def:additive-representation}.

A family is said to have \emph{bounded additive dimension} if this
number is bounded independently of the planning horizon.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
The term \enquote{additive dimension} used here should not be confused
with the notion bearing the same name in  \textit{additive combinatorics} and
\textit{additive number theory}.   The notion introduced in
Definition~\ref{def:additive dimension} is specific to the present
framework.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:additive-compression}
Suppose that the boundary resource profile admits a $p$-dimensional
additive representation. Then every boundary sum set
$\mathcal{A}(J)$ satisfies $\mathcal{A}(J)
\subseteq
\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$ for all $J\subseteq\mathcal{T}$.  Moreover,
\begin{equation*}
|\widehat{\mathcal{A}}|
\leq
\prod_{i=1}^{p}
\left(
2T^{c_i+1}+1
\right). 
\end{equation*}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Let $a\in\mathcal{A}(J)$. Then $a=\sum_{u\in J}b_u$  for some $b_u\in\mathcal{B}_u$. By~\eqref{eq:aggregate-representation}, $a
=
\sum_{i=1}^{p}\theta_i\beta_i$,  where the aggregate coordinates satisfy $|\beta_i|\leq T^{c_i+1}$. 
 
Furthermore, because all production boundaries are nonnegative, we have  $0\leq a\leq U^\Sigma$. Therefore, $a\in\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$. 
 

For each coordinate $\beta_i$, there are at most $2T^{c_i+1}+1$  integer values satisfying its bound. Hence, the total number of
coordinate vectors is at most $\prod_{i=1}^{p}
\left(
2T^{c_i+1}+1
\right)$. 
 
Different vectors may generate the same value, so this is also an
upper bound on
$|\widehat{\mathcal{A}}|$.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:grid-compression}
If the boundary resource profile admits a $p$-dimensional additive
representation, then $G\subseteq\widehat{G}$.   Moreover,
\begin{equation}
|\widehat{G}|
\leq
2(T+1)
\prod_{i=1}^{p}
\left(
2T^{c_i+1}+1
\right).
\label{eq:aggregate-grid-cardinality}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Let $s\in G$. Then $s\in G_t$ for some
$t\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{0\}$. If $s\in G_t^+$, then by definition $s
=
D_j+a$ for some $0\leq j\leq t$ and some $a\in
\mathcal{A}(\{j+1,\ldots,t\})$.  By Lemma~\ref{lem:additive-compression}, $a\in\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$,  and therefore $s\in\widehat{G}$. 
 

Similarly, if $s\in G_t^-$, then $s
=
D_j-a$ for some $t\leq j\leq T$ and $a\in
\mathcal{A}(\{t+1,\ldots,j\})$.  Again, $a\in\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$,  and hence $s\in\widehat{G}$.  Thus, $G\subseteq\widehat{G}$.
 

For every cumulative demand anchor $D_j$, there are at most
$2|\widehat{\mathcal{A}}|$ values corresponding to the two signs.
Hence, $|\widehat{G}|
\leq
2(T+1)|\widehat{\mathcal{A}}|$.  

The result follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:additive-compression}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:LiLi}
Li and Li \cite{LiLi2016} provide a general polynomial solvability
framework based on a fixed set of time-independent
\emph{special replenishment quantities} and the property that at most
one period between consecutive regeneration periods uses a quantity
outside this set. A fixed collection $\{q_1,\ldots,q_R\}$ of boundary values fits naturally within the present framework by taking the $q_r$ as basis values and using count coordinates. Hence, the setting with a finite set of special quantities constitutes an important special case of the additive representation considered here.

The converse need not hold. Bounded additive dimension does not require the number of distinct boundary values to remain fixed. For example, a fixed-degree polynomial capacity profile $C_t=\sum_{\ell=0}^{d}\gamma_\ell t^\ell$ may contain $T$ distinct capacity values, while every capacity sum is described by the fixed collection of power sum coordinates $\sum_{t\in S}t^\ell$ for  $\ell=0,\ldots,d$ (cf., Section~\ref{subsec:polynomial-capacities}). Thus, additive dimension captures structured resource families that need not admit a fixed list of special replenishment quantities.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:general-polynomiality}
Consider a family $\mathfrak{I}$ of feasible dynamic lot-sizing
instances of the form~$\mathcal P$. If the corresponding
boundary resource profiles have bounded additive dimension, then
$\mathfrak{I}$ satisfies the polynomial grid condition.  Consequently, every such instance can be solved exactly in polynomial
time by the GDP algorithm.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Let $p$ denote the bounded additive dimension, and let
$c_1,\ldots,c_p$ be the fixed exponents of an additive
representation. By Lemma~\ref{lem:grid-compression}, the exact additive grid is
contained in the grid envelope $\widehat{G}$, whose cardinality
satisfies~\eqref{eq:aggregate-grid-cardinality}. Since $p$ and $c_1,\ldots,c_p$ are fixed independently of $T$, this
quantity is polynomial in $T$. More precisely, $|\widehat{G}|
=
O
\left(
T^{
1+\sum_{i=1}^{p}(c_i+1)
}
\right)$.  

By Definition \ref{def:additive-representation}, the basis values and coordinate maps are polynomial-time computable and have polynomially bounded encoding lengths. The additive envelope $\widehat{\mathcal{A}}$ can therefore be generated by enumerating all
integer vectors $(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_p)$ satisfying $|\beta_i|\leq T^{c_i+1}$ for all $i=1,\ldots,p$, and evaluating $\sum_{i=1}^{p}\theta_i\beta_i$ exactly. 
 

Because the number of such vectors is polynomial, the additive
envelope can be generated in polynomial time. Combining each retained
value with the $T+1$ cumulative demand anchors and the two possible
signs generates $\widehat{G}$ in polynomial time.

Therefore, $\widehat{G}$ satisfies the polynomial grid condition. Moreover, by Proposition~\ref{prop:polynomial grid-principle}, the GDP algorithm solves the problem in polynomial time.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:concave-extreme point}
Fix a setup vector $y\in\{0,1\}^{T}$. If $c_t$ and $H_t$ are concave for every $t$, then the fixed-setup problem associated with $\mathcal P^{\mathrm{conc}}$ admits an optimal solution that is an extreme point of $\mathcal{X}(y)$.
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
For a fixed setup vector $y$, the feasible production vectors belong to the polytope $\mathcal{X}(y)$ defined in \eqref{eq:fixed-setup-polytope}. Using $I_t=\sum_{u=1}^{t}x_u-D_t$,  the objective, apart from the constant setup term $\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_ty_t$, can be written as
\begin{equation*}
\Psi_y(x)
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}
\left[
c_t(x_t)
+
H_t
\left(
\sum_{u=1}^{t}x_u-D_t
\right)
\right]. 
\end{equation*}
Since each $c_t$ and $H_t$ is concave and the inventory levels are affine functions of $x$, the function $\Psi_y$ is concave on
$\mathcal{X}(y)$.

Let $x^\star$ be an optimal solution. Since $\mathcal{X}(y)$ is a polytope, $x^\star$ can be expressed as a convex combination of its
extreme points: $x^\star = \sum_{q=1}^{m}\lambda_q v^q$ where $\lambda_q\geq0$ and  $\sum_{q=1}^{m}\lambda_q=1$.
 
By concavity,
$$
\Psi_y(x^\star)
\geq
\sum_{q=1}^{m}
\lambda_q\Psi_y(v^q).
$$
Therefore, at least one extreme point $v^q$ satisfies
$$
\Psi_y(v^q)
\leq
\Psi_y(x^\star).
$$
Since $x^\star$ is optimal, equality must hold. Hence, an optimal extreme point exists.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:concave-grid}
Suppose that $c_t$ and $H_t$ are concave for every
$t\in\mathcal{T}$. Then problem~$\mathcal P^{\mathrm{conc}}$ admits an
optimal solution such that, in every regeneration interval, at most
one production quantity is strictly between its production
boundaries. Consequently, there exists an optimal solution whose
cumulative production trajectory satisfies $P_t\in G_t$ for all $t\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{0\}$,   where $G_t$ is the same additive grid defined in
Section~\ref{sec:grid-theory}.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Let $y^\star$ be the setup vector of an optimal solution of problem~$\mathcal P^{\mathrm{conc}}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:concave-extreme point}, there exists an optimal production vector $x^\star$ that is an extreme point of $\mathcal{X}(y^\star)$.

Theorem \ref{thm:extreme point} therefore implies that, in every regeneration interval, all but at most one production quantity belong to $\mathcal{B}_t=\{0,L_t,U_t\}$.

The proof of the MGT is purely structural and applies to any solution satisfying this boundary property. Hence, the corresponding cumulative production trajectory satisfies $P_t\in G_t$ for all  $t\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{0\}$.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:concave-polynomiality}
Consider a family of instances of
problem~$\mathcal P^{\mathrm{conc}}$ whose boundary resource profiles have
bounded additive dimension. If the concave cost functions can be
evaluated exactly in polynomial time, then the family is solvable
exactly in polynomial time by GDP.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:concave-grid}, an optimal solution exists on the
same additive grid as in the linear cost model. Moreover, by Theorem~\ref{thm:general-polynomiality}, bounded additive dimension
provides a polynomially constructible grid envelope
$\widehat{G}$ of polynomial cardinality. 

Applying the recurrence~\eqref{eq:concave-grid-dp} to the feasible states $\widehat{G}\cap[D_t,D_T]$ in period $t$ examines at most $|\widehat{G}|^2$ predecessor--successor pairs per period.
Therefore, the total number of transitions is polynomial in the input size. Since every transition cost can also be evaluated in polynomial time, the complete algorithm is polynomial.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:uncapacitated}
The uncapacitated single-item dynamic lot-sizing problem with linear costs can be solved by GDP in $O(T^2)$ time and $O(T)$ working memory for computing the optimal value.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
The common cumulative production grid contains $O(T)$ states. The
accelerated recurrence of Section~\ref{sec:grid-dp} therefore requires
$O(T|H^{\mathrm{unc}}|)=O(T^2)$ time.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:constant capacity}
The single-item dynamic lot-sizing problem with constant capacity can be solved by the GDP algorithm in $O(T^3)$ time and $O(T^2)$ working memory for computing the optimal value when the common grid $H^{C}$ is used.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The grid envelope contains $O(T^2)$ states. Once sorted, Proposition~\ref{prop:grid-dp-complexity} yields $O(T|H^{C}|) = O(T^3)$ time and $O(T^2)$ memory.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:constant-moq}
The uncapacitated single-item dynamic lot-sizing problem with a constant minimum order quantity can be solved by the GDP algorithm in $O(T^3)$ time and $O(T^2)$ working memory for computing the optimal value.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The set $H^{L}$ is a grid envelope of cardinality $O(T^2)$. Proposition~\ref{prop:grid-dp-complexity} therefore gives an $O(T^3)$ implementation.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:constant capacity-moq}
The single-item dynamic lot-sizing problem with constant capacity $C$ and constant minimum order quantity $L$ can be solved by the GDP algorithm in $O(T^4)$ time and $O(T^3)$ working memory for computing the optimal value.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The grid envelope $H^{L,C}$ contains $O(T^3)$ cumulative production states. The result follows directly from Proposition~\ref{prop:grid-dp-complexity}.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The terminal inventory conventions are not identical across all of these models. The formulation considered in this paper imposes $I_T=0$. Okhrin and Richter \cite{OkhrinRichter2011a} use the same zero-terminal-inventory convention, whereas minimum-order-quantity models allowing positive terminal inventory are also considered by Hellion, Mangione, and Penz \cite{HellionMangionePenz2012} and Park and Klabjan \cite{ParkKlabjan2015}.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:fixed-capacity-levels}
For every fixed $R$, the capacitated lot-sizing problem in which $C_t\in\{q_1,\ldots,q_R\}$ for all $t$ is solvable by the GDP algorithm in $O(T^{R+2})$ time.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:polynomial capacity}
For every fixed degree $d$, the capacitated lot-sizing problem with capacity profile~\eqref{eq:polynomial capacity} is solvable by the GDP algorithm in $O
\left(
T^{
2+\frac{(d+1)(d+2)}{2}
}
\right)$  time.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:seasonal-capacity}
For every fixed period $q$, the capacitated lot-sizing problem with capacity profile~\eqref{eq:periodic-capacity} is solvable in polynomial time by the GDP algorithm.
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:piecewise polynomial}
If both the number $R$ of pieces and the maximum polynomial degree
$d$ are fixed independently of $T$, then the capacitated lot-sizing
problem with capacity profile~\eqref{eq:piecewise polynomial capacity}
is solvable by the GDP algorithm in $O
\left(
T^{
2+
R\frac{(d+1)(d+2)}{2}
}
\right)$ time.
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
